_comment: DBE Grade 12 Accounting P1, November 2024. Questions + marking-guideline
answers extracted from the text layer of the PDFs in this directory
(paper1.pdf, paper1_memo.pdf) and cross-checked by recomputing figures.
Schema follows past_papers/maths/grade11/2018/paper.json. One addition:
an optional 'information' field (array of verbatim lines) carries the
INFORMATION / pre-adjustment data block of each main question; it is
attached to the FIRST sub-question of that main question and applies to
all sub-questions with the same main-question number.
Sub-parts that the paper prints as unnumbered bullets are given suffixed
refs (e.g. Q2.3a, Q3.4a) in printed order.
memo_working reproduces the marking guideline's figures and allocation
notation (one mark / two marks / one part correct / operation / method
mark). The memo's tick glyphs are images and did not survive text
extraction; their per-figure placement is therefore described in words,
not drawn.
The paper's instruction table: Q1 Company Financial Statements 55 marks
45 min; Q2 Cash Flow Statement and Financial Indicators 35 marks 25 min;
Q3 Interpretation of Financial Information 45 marks 35 min; Q4 Corporate
Governance 15 marks 15 min. A Financial Indicator Formula Sheet is
attached to the paper (standard NSC sheet, not transcribed here).

questions.text: Refer to Information B (i) for fixed assets. Calculate: Depreciation on equipment on 29 February 2024. (The information relates to Ivory Park Ltd for the financial year ended 29 February 2024.)
information: A. Balances/totals, among others, that appeared in the books on:
Equipment: No equipment was bought or sold during the year.

Vehicles: An old vehicle was traded in on 1 September 2023 for a new vehicle, costing R320 000. The trade-in value received was R153 660. The following extract of the vehicle sold was taken from the Fixed Asset Register:
Cost price: R240 000    Date purchased: 1 July 2021
Rate of depreciation: 20% p.a. on the diminishing-balance method
(columns: FINANCIAL YEAR END | DEPRECIATION | ACCUMULATED DEPRECIATION)
Vehicles are depreciated at 20% p.a. on the diminishing-balance method. Depreciation on the old remaining vehicles was R132 720.
(ii) The company maintains a mark-up of 60% on cost. Note that goods costing R115 000 (included in cost of sales) were sold at a mark-up of 40% on cost to internal employees.
(iii) Physical stocktaking on 29 February 2024 revealed the following: Trading stock, R647 100; Packing material used during the financial year, R58 700
(iv) Provision for bad debts must be adjusted to 5% of the outstanding debtors.
(v) Monthly insurance premiums were fixed for the past three years and were paid up to 31 May 2024.
(vi) A tenant is renting an office from Ivory Park Ltd. Rent for this office has been received up until 30 April 2024. Rent was decreased by 8% on 1 December 2023 on the office rented.

(vii) One employee was omitted from the Salaries Journal of February 2024. His net monthly salary was R19 340 after 35% deductions were made for his pension and personal tax and R2 500 deducted for medical aid. The employer contributes 10% of his gross salary on behalf of employees towards pension.

(viii) The company had two directors who received a combined annual fee of R1 065 200 after their monthly fees were increased by R5 800 each on 1 August 2023. A third director joined the company on 1 November 2023 and received the same monthly fee as the other directors, excluding the increase of R5 800 per month.
(ix) Net profit after tax, R992 160, was calculated after taking into account all the adjustments above. Income tax is calculated at 28% of the net profit.

questions.text: Calculate: Cost price of vehicles on 29 February 2024
questions.memo_answer: 1 330 000 (one part correct)
questions.memo_working: 1 250 000 (one mark) - 240 000 (one mark) + 320 000 (one mark) = 1 330 000 (one method mark). OR shown as a Vehicles ledger account: debit 1 250 000, 320 000; credit 240 000, balance 1 330 000. If a working is shown as a final answer, award working mark only.

questions.text: Calculate: Depreciation on vehicles on 29 February 2024
questions.memo_answer: 181 360 (one part correct; should include R132 720)
questions.memo_working: Depreciation on new vehicle: 320 000 x [20/100 x 6/12] = 32 000 (one part correct). Depreciation on vehicle traded in: [240 000 - 73 600] = 166 400; 166 400 x [20/100 x 6/12] = 16 640 (one part correct). Depreciation on remaining vehicles 132 720. Total 32 000 + 16 640 + 132 720 = 181 360.

questions.text: Calculate: Profit/Loss on vehicle traded in on 1 September 2023
questions.topic: Company Financial Statements - Fixed Assets (Asset Disposal)
questions.memo_answer: 3 900 profit (one part correct)
questions.memo_working: Accumulated depreciation on disposal: 73 600 (one mark) + 16 640 (one method mark, see 1.1.3) = 90 240. 240 000 - 90 240 - 153 660 = carrying value 149 760 (three marks) vs trade-in 153 660 -> profit 3 900. OR Asset disposal account: 240 000 (one mark) debit; 90 240 (one mark + one method mark) and 153 660 (one mark) credit; profit 3 900 (one method mark). If a working is shown as a final answer, award working mark/s only. NOTE: The relevant amounts calculated in 1.1.1-1.1.4 must be transferred to QUESTION 1.2, the Statement of Comprehensive Income.

questions.text: Complete the Statement of Comprehensive Income for the year ended 29 February 2024. NOTE: Some amounts are provided in the ANSWER BOOK.
questions.topic: Company Financial Statements - Statement of Comprehensive Income
questions.memo_answer: Sales 7 626 440; Cost of sales (4 780 900); Gross profit 2 845 540; Other income 1 902 000; Gross operating income 4 747 540; Operating expenses (3 371 340); Operating profit 1 376 200; Interest income 151 200; Profit before interest expense 1 527 400; Interest expense (149 400); Net profit before tax 1 378 000; Income tax (385 840); Net profit after tax 992 160
questions.memo_working: Sales: [4 780 900 x 1,6] = 7 649 440 - [115 000 x 0,2] = 23 000 -> 7 626 440 (one part correct; both figures must be added/subtracted) OR [4 665 900 x 1,6] = 7 465 440 (two marks) + [115 000 x 1,4] = 161 000 (two marks). Cost of sales (4 780 900). Gross profit = Sales - Cost of sales = 2 845 540 (6 marks to here). Other income (operation) 1 902 000: Service fee income 1 757 700; Profit on sale of asset 3 900 (see 1.1.4; if calculated as loss in 1.1.4 award method mark under operating expenses); Rent income 158 100 - 21 390 [10 695 x 2] = 136 710 (one part correct) OR 104 625 + 32 085; Provision for bad debts adjustment 3 690 (should be shown as an income). Gross operating income = GP + OI = 4 747 540 (9 marks in this block). Operating expenses (operation) (3 371 340): Audit fees 79 000; Sundry operating expenses 119 900; Bad debts 24 780; Packing material 58 700; Trading stock deficit 7 400 (should be shown as an expense); Insurance 100 800 - 20 160 [100 800 x 3/15 OR 6 720 x 3] = 80 640 (one part correct; OR 100 800 x 12/15); Salaries and wages 1 425 600 + 33 600 + 3 360 = 1 462 560 (one part correct; workings [21 840 + 11 760] and [gross salary x 10%]); Directors' fees 1 065 200 + 164 000 [41 000 x 4] = 1 229 200 (one part correct); Depreciation [127 800 + 181 360, see 1.1.1 and 1.1.3; both figures should be added to award method mark] = 309 160 (18 marks in this block). Operating profit = GOI - OE = 1 376 200. Interest income 151 200 (balancing figure, accept a negative figure). Profit before interest expense = NPBT + interest expense = 1 527 400. Interest expense (149 400). Net profit before tax = NPAT + income tax = 1 378 000. Income tax = NPAT x 28/72 = (385 840). Net profit after tax 992 160. Penalties: -1 foreign items (max -2) i.e. Statement of Financial Position items; -1 presentation (max -1).

questions.text: Prepare the Retained Income Note for the year ended 29 February 2024. (The information relates to Eybers Ltd for the financial year ended 29 February 2024.)
questions.topic: Cash Flow Statement - Retained Income Note
questions.memo_answer: Balance at the beginning of the year 573 720; Net profit after tax 1 862 150; Repurchase of shares (64 600); Ordinary share dividends (744 860): Interim dividend 416 000, Final dividend 328 860; Balance at the end of the year 1 626 410
questions.memo_working: Net profit after tax: 744 860 / 40% (dividend pay-out rate) = 1 862 150 (one part correct) OR 744 860 x 100/40. Repurchase of shares (64 600) (ignore brackets). Ordinary share dividends (744 860): Interim 416 000; Final = OSD - interim = 328 860. Balance at end 1 626 410 (one part correct; check operation; shares repurchased and OSD must be subtracted). -1P if no details (max -1). Memo alternative version: Net profit after tax (1 458 167 x 1,175) = 1 713 346 with closing balance 1 477 606, all other lines identical.
questions.memo_note: The memo prints two accepted versions of the note. The primary version derives NPAT from the 40% pay-out rate (1 862 150). The alternative shows 1 458 167 x 1,175 = 1 713 346; the memo gives no derivation for 1 458 167.

questions.text: Complete the Cash Flow Statement for the year ended 29 February 2024.
questions.memo_answer: Operating activities: Taxation paid (573 325); Dividends paid (620 000). Financing activities: New shares issued 4 000 000; Shares repurchased (323 000); Loan repaid (480 000). Net change in cash and cash equivalents 296 460; Cash and cash equivalents at the beginning of the year (106 680); Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year 189 780
questions.memo_working: Taxation paid: 44 675 + 462 000 + 66 650 = (573 325) (one part correct; OR -44 675 - 462 000 - 66 650). Dividends paid: (1 200 000 x 17/100) = 204 000 + [744 860 - 328 860] = 416 000 -> (620 000) (one part correct). [Operating-activities block: 8 marks.] New shares issued 4 000 000. Shares repurchased: (34 000 x 7,60) = 258 400 + (34 000 x 1,90) = 64 600 (see 2.1) -> (323 000) (one part correct; both figures added). Loan repaid (480 000) (if no bracket, award one mark). [Financing-activities block: 6 marks.] Cash and cash equivalents at the beginning of the year (106 680) (if no bracket, award one mark). Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year 189 780 (operation) [3 marks]. Notes: * one part correct, reflected as an outflow (brackets); -1 poor presentation (max -1); be alert to alternative workings such as ledger account or use of brackets or signs reversed; for use of reversed signs, ensure that only one option is marked consistently; if no brackets, assume answer is an inflow of cash - award marks for workings only; if a workings amount is shown as a final figure, award the mark/s allocated, ignore the brackets; if correct figure is shown without brackets or workings, award all working marks only, not final mark. The memo's printed layout leaves the Cash generated from operations, Interest paid and investing-activities lines blank (pre-printed/not examined here).

questions.text: Profitability: Quote TWO financial indicators with figures and trends to indicate that the company is managing its expenses well. (The information relates to Winston Ltd for the year ended 29 February 2024. NOTE: Where comments or explanations are required, you should quote financial indicators and trends with figures and give a reason or an explanation for the financial indicators quoted.)
questions.memo_answer: Any TWO of: % operating expenses on sales has decreased / improved (from 19%) to 14% / by 5%-points / by 26,3%; % operating profit on sales has increased / improved (from 12%) to 18% / by 6%-points / by 50%; % net profit before tax on sales has increased / improved (from 11%) to 19% / by 8%-points / by 72,7%. Do not accept mark-up %. (Financial indicators: 2 marks; figures and trends: 2 marks)
information: The chief executive officer (CEO), Shakira Solomon, was appointed on 1 October 2023.
She was awarded a one-year contract, on probation.
Grant Waters, the majority shareholder, was instrumental in appointing the CEO on 1 October 2023.
B. Share capital and rights issue:
3 000 000 shares were already in issue on 1 March 2023.
Grant Waters' shareholding: He is the majority shareholder and owned 1 620 000 of the issued shares on 1 March 2023.

Rights issue: On 31 October 2023, each shareholder was offered 10 shares for every 50 shares that they owned at a reduced price. All shareholders exercised this right. No other shares were issued or repurchased during the financial year.
C. Extract from the Notes and Statement of Financial Position as at: (columns: 29 Feb. 2024 | 28 Feb. 2023)
D. Financial indicators, market prices of shares, interest rates and other financial data: (columns: 29 Feb. 2024 | 28 Feb. 2023)
% net profit before tax on sales            19% | 11%
Net asset value per share             564 cents | 460 cents
Market value per share                950 cents | 820 cents
% growth (drop) in net asset value per share +15,9% | -8,9%

questions.text: Dividend pay-out policy: Comment on the dividend pay-out policy of the company. Explain why this is a responsible change in policy. Provide ONE point.
questions.topic: Interpretation of Financial Information - Dividend Policy
questions.memo_answer: Figures and trend (1 mark): It decreased (from 86%) to 60% / by 26%-points / by 30,2%. Explanation (2 marks, part mark for unclear/incomplete answers): Funds have been retained for future expansion purposes / shareholders will benefit in the future as funds have been set aside / protect the cash flow of the business.

questions.text: Earnings and returns: Explain whether the shareholders should be satisfied or not with the earnings per share and returns on average shareholders' equity of the company. Quote TWO financial indicators with figures.
questions.topic: Interpretation of Financial Information - Returns and Earnings
questions.memo_answer: EPS: increased (from 104 cents) to 112 cents / by 8 cents / by 7,7%; shareholders should be happy as it shows an increase in the profitability of the company. ROSHE: increased (from 11%) to 20% / by 9%-points / by 81,8%; shareholders should be satisfied because ROSHE (20%) is greater than the interest rate on fixed deposit (7,5%).

questions.text: Financing strategies and gearing: Refer to Information C. The directors decided to buy new fixed assets in 2024 to enhance the company. Identify the TWO main sources (over R1m) that were used to finance this purchase. Provide figures.
questions.memo_answer: Shares issued (sold), R2 970 000 (from 28 800 000) to 31 770 000 / by 10,3%; Increase in loan, R3 513 000 (from 9 400 000) to 12 913 000 / by 37,4%. Do not accept: sale of fixed assets / cash and cash equivalents. (Source: 2 marks; figures: 2 marks)

questions.text: Explain how the decisions affected the risk and gearing of the company. Quote TWO financial indicators with figures.
questions.topic: Interpretation of Financial Information - Gearing and Risk
questions.memo_answer: Debt/equity ratio: decreased / improved (from 0,5 : 1) to 0,2 : 1 / by 0,3 : 1; company still has a low financial risk. Return on average capital employed (ROTCE): increased (from 15%) to 24% / by 9%-points / by 60%; company has positive gearing / ROTCE (24%) is greater than interest rate on loan (12%).

questions.text: Grant Waters' % shareholding, rights issue and shares repurchased: Refer to Information B. Calculate the number of shares that Grant bought through the rights issue on 31 October 2023.
questions.memo_answer: 324 000 shares
questions.memo_working: 1 620 000 / 50 = 32 400 (two marks) x 10 = 324 000 (mark awarded if x 10). Check numerator / denominator.

questions.text: Calculate Grant's % shareholding after the rights issue on 29 February 2024.
questions.memo_answer: 54% (one part correct)

questions.text: Calculate the total amount that Grant spent on the shares he acquired through the rights issue. NOTE: No shares were repurchased during the financial year.
questions.memo_answer: R1 603 800 (one part correct)
questions.memo_working: 324 000 (see above) x R4,95 (see 3.4: 2 970 000 / 600 000) = 1 603 800. OR 2 970 000 (see 3.4, one method mark) - 1 366 200 (276 000 x 4,95; one mark + one method mark). Note: award method mark if calculations are provided for R4,95.

questions.text: Grant intends to convince the board of directors to repurchase shares from him in the next financial year at R12 per share. Explain why the other board members would probably vote against this transaction proposed by Grant. Provide TWO points (with figures).
questions.topic: Interpretation of Financial Information - Share Repurchase
questions.memo_answer: Any TWO valid points with figures (part mark for unclear/incomplete answers): The repurchase price of (R12 / 1 200 cents) exceeds the market value per share of 950 cents / by 250 cents; The repurchase price of (R12 / 1 200 cents) exceeds the NAV per share of 564 cents / by 636 cents; He is taking advantage of his status as the majority shareholder, 54% (see above) / this constitutes self-enrichment due to his position as the majority shareholder by 54%.

questions.text: Role of the CEO: Explain TWO characteristics that shareholders would expect of a good CEO.
questions.topic: Corporate Governance - Role of the CEO
questions.memo_answer: Any TWO valid explanations: Ability to set and communicate a clear vision of the company / strong communication skills to effectively convey important information; Maintain transparency with all stakeholders; Ability to deliver consistent financial performance / understand financial management; Ability to attract, develop and retain top talent; Committed to ethical business practice with high standard of integrity; Adapt quickly to change / respond to unexpected challenges; Ability to identify and address the needs of various stakeholders / make well-informed decisions to manage risk and drive positive outcomes; Creative in identifying new opportunities / allocate resources effectively to remain competitive in the market.

questions.text: Apart from the factors and financial indicators covered in the previous questions, identify and explain TWO other points indicating that the company is well managed by the CEO. Quote figures.
questions.topic: Interpretation of Financial Information - Liquidity and Solvency
questions.memo_answer: Any TWO (financial indicators with figures and trend, 2 marks; explanation, 2 marks): Solvency ratio increased / improved (from 2,8 : 1) to 3,8 : 1, the business has a stronger financial position; Current ratio increased / improved (from 1,6 : 1) to 2,5 : 1 and the business's ability to pay its short-term debts has strengthened; Acid-test ratio increased / improved (from 1,2 : 1) to 1,9 : 1 and the business has enough cash to cover its short-term debts. Do not accept mark-up %.

questions.text: Explain the role of an independent external auditor. Provide ONE point. (You are provided with an extract of the independent external audit report of Valiant Ltd, presented to the shareholders at the Annual General Meeting. NOTE: In your answers, do NOT repeat your responses in the different questions.)
questions.memo_answer: Any suitable relevant response: Provides an unbiased audit report on the financial statements of the company; Presents an opinion on the fair presentation of the financial statements; Protects the interest of the shareholders/public.
information: Extract from the independent external auditor's report on the financial statements of Valiant Ltd:
Audit Opinion: In our opinion the financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of the company as at 29 February 2024 ...
Basis for Audit Opinion: ... and the audit evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion.

questions.text: Choose the correct word from those in brackets. Write the answer in the ANSWER BOOK and explain your choice. Valiant Ltd received a/an (qualified/unqualified/disclaimer of opinion) audit report.
questions.memo_answer: Unqualified (1 mark). Explanation (1 mark), any suitable relevant response: No errors / problems / irregularities were discovered; Opinion indicates that the financial statements fairly present the financial situation of the company.

questions.text: What kind of audit evidence does the independent external auditor examine to verify the fixed assets of a company? Provide TWO points.
questions.memo_answer: Any suitable relevant response (2 x 2 marks): Confirm the physical existence of items listed on the fixed assets register; Check if calculations of depreciation are correct / check the correct depreciation rate was used; Check the invoice/receipt against the cost price written on the fixed asset register if they are the same; Check if correct procedure followed in procurement of new fixed assets / check if correct procedures were followed in disposing of fixed assets; Check the registration certificate / title deed to confirm ownership. Responses for one mark: Check the fixed asset register; Check the logbook; Verify source documents.

questions.text: What are the implications of this audit report for the following: Directors; Shareholders. State ONE point in each case.
questions.memo_answer: Directors (any suitable relevant response, 2 marks): Will be reappointed by the shareholders; Improves their credentials / reputation. Shareholders (any suitable relevant response, 2 marks): Satisfied that their investment is safe; It will encourage further investment in the company. Note: 1. Check the type of audit report identified in 4.2 and mark 4.4 accordingly. 2. Disregard the audit report chosen in 4.2, if the candidate's answer in 4.4 matches the marking guideline above.

questions.text: State THREE possible consequences for the independent external auditor if he was influenced by the directors of the company to deliberately provide the shareholders with an incorrect audit report.
questions.memo_answer: Any suitable relevant response, accept one-word answers (3 x 1 mark). As employee: deregistered / struck off the roll by IRBA (accounting body) / loss of professional licence / revocation of his certificate; disciplinary hearing / suspended (during investigation) / fired by his employer / fined / imprisonment (arrested); sued by shareholders (company) for negligence (financial loss) / bad reputation to his name. For the auditing company (auditor's employer): lose clients / removed as auditors by clients / loss of employment to staff as client base decreases / acquiring contracts will be challenging in the future / bad image of the company.
